outcomes.text: Describe how light microscopes and staining are used to view cells.
Explain how the main parts of plant, animal and bacterial cells fit their functions.
Explain how electron microscopy deepened understanding of sub-cellular structures.

topics.title: B1.2 What happens in cells (and what do cells need)?

outcomes.text: Describe DNA as a polymer.
Describe DNA as two strands forming a double helix.
Describe experiments that investigate enzyme-catalysed reactions.
Explain how enzymes act, including the active site and effect of conditions.
Describe cellular respiration as a universal process happening continuously in living cells.
Describe respiration as an exothermic reaction.
Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
Explain how sugars build and break down carbohydrates.
Explain how amino acids build and break down proteins.
Explain how fatty acids and glycerol build and break down lipids.
Describe photosynthetic organisms as the main producers of food and biomass.
Describe the process of photosynthesis, its reactants and products.
Describe photosynthesis as an endothermic reaction.
Describe experiments that investigate photosynthesis.
Explain how temperature, light and carbon dioxide level affect photosynthesis rate.
Explain how these three factors interact to limit the rate.
Explain how substances cross cell membranes by diffusion, osmosis and active transport.
Describe mitosis in growth, including the cell cycle.
Explain why cells differentiate.
Recall that stem cells exist in embryonic and adult animals and meristems in plants.
Describe what stem cells and meristems do.
Describe how embryonic and adult stem cells differ.
Explain why large organisms need exchange surfaces and transport systems, using surface area to volume ratio.
Describe substances transported in and out of various organisms.
Describe the human circulatory system.
Explain how heart and blood vessel structure suits function.
Explain how red blood cells and plasma suit their transport jobs.
Explain how plants take up water and minerals, linking root hair cells to function.
Describe transpiration and translocation.
Explain how xylem and phloem suit their functions.
Explain how environmental factors change water uptake in plants.
Describe how a potometer investigates water uptake.

topics.title: B3.1 Coordination and control - the nervous system

outcomes.text: Describe the structure of the nervous system.
Explain how its components produce a coordinated response.
Explain how a reflex arc's structure relates to its function.

topics.title: B3.2 Coordination and control - the endocrine system

outcomes.text: Describe how the endocrine system coordinates and controls the body.
Explain the roles of thyroxine and adrenaline.
Describe the role of hormones in reproduction, including the menstrual cycle.
Explain how FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone interact in the cycle.
Explain hormones in contraception and evaluate hormonal and non-hormonal methods.
Explain hormones in treating infertility.
Explain why a constant internal environment is needed.
Explain how insulin controls blood sugar.
Explain how glucagon works with insulin.
Compare type 1 and type 2 diabetes and their treatment.
Recall that materials cycle between abiotic and biotic parts of an ecosystem.
Explain the role of microorganisms in cycling materials.
Explain the importance of the carbon and water cycles.
Describe levels of organisation in an ecosystem.
Explain how abiotic and biotic factors affect communities.
Describe interdependence and competition in a community.

units.title: Topic B5: Genes, inheritance and selection

outcomes.text: Explain terms such as gamete, chromosome, gene, allele, dominant, recessive, genotype and phenotype.
Describe the genome as an organism's entire genetic material.
Describe how genome and environment shape phenotype.
Recall that variants arise from mutations, most having no effect.
Explain the terms haploid and diploid.
Explain how meiosis halves chromosome number to form gametes.
Explain single gene inheritance in homozygous and heterozygous crosses.
Predict single gene cross results with Punnett squares.
Describe human sex determination with a genetic cross.
Recall that most features result from multiple genes.
State that populations usually have extensive genetic variation.
Describe how biological developments have affected classification.
Explain how natural selection of best-suited variants drives evolution.
Describe evolution as change in inherited characteristics over time, possibly forming new species.
Describe evidence for evolution such as fossils and antibiotic-resistant bacteria.

topics.title: B6.1 Monitoring and maintaining the environment

outcomes.text: Explain how to run a field investigation of distribution and abundance.
Describe human impacts on ecosystems and biodiversity.
Explain benefits and challenges of maintaining biodiversity.
Explain the impact of selectively breeding food plants and animals.
Describe genetic engineering as modifying an organism's genome.
Describe the main steps of genetic engineering.
Explain benefits and risks of gene technology in agriculture.
Describe the relationship between health and disease.
Describe types of disease.
Describe how different diseases interact.
Explain how pathogens spread disease in animals and plants.
Explain how the spread of disease is reduced or prevented.
Describe a common human infection, a plant disease and sexually transmitted infections.
Explain how white blood cells and platelets suit their defence jobs.
Describe the body's non-specific defences.
Explain the immune system's role in defence.
Explain how vaccines and medicines prevent and treat disease.
Describe how new medicines are discovered and developed.
Recall that many non-communicable diseases come from several interacting factors.
Evaluate treatments for cardiovascular disease.
Analyse how lifestyle affects non-communicable disease at local, national and global levels.
Describe cancer as changes in cells causing uncontrolled growth.
Discuss benefits and risks of stem cells in medicine.
Explain benefits and risks of gene technology in medicine.
Discuss why understanding the human genome matters for medicine.
Describe the particle model of states of matter and changes of state.
Use particles to explain physical versus chemical changes.
Explain the limits of the particle model when particles are drawn as inelastic spheres.
Describe how and why the atomic model changed.
Describe the atom as a small positive nucleus with surrounding electrons.
Recall the typical size of atoms and small molecules.
Recall relative charges and masses of protons, neutrons and electrons.
Calculate numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in atoms and ions.

units.title: Topic C2: Elements, compounds and mixtures

outcomes.text: Explain what purity means scientifically versus in everyday use.
Use melting points to distinguish pure from impure substances.
Calculate relative formula masses.
Deduce empirical formulae from atom ratios or diagrams, and the reverse.
Explain that useful materials are often formulated mixtures such as alloys.
Describe filtration, crystallisation, simple and fractional distillation.
Suggest suitable purification techniques for given substances.
Describe paper and thin layer chromatography.
Recall the stationary and mobile phases in chromatography.
Interpret chromatograms, including measuring Rf.
Suggest chromatographic methods for distinguishing pure from impure substances.
Describe metals and non-metals and explain how their properties differ.
Explain how atomic structure of metals and non-metals relates to Periodic Table position.
Explain how position relates to electron arrangement and atomic number.
Explain how elements' reactions relate to electron arrangement.
Explain how atomic number refined Mendeleev's table.
Describe and compare bonds in ionic compounds and simple molecules.
Explain bonding through electrostatic forces and electron transfer or sharing.
Draw dot and cross diagrams for simple covalent and binary ionic substances.
Describe limitations of different representations of bonding.
Recall that carbon forms four covalent bonds.
Explain how carbon's chains and rings create many organic compounds.
Explain properties of diamond, graphite, fullerenes and graphene from structure and bonding.
Use energy transfers and bond strengths to explain change-of-state temperatures.
Use data to predict states of substances.
Explain how bulk properties of different material types relate to their bonds.
Use symbols to write formulae of elements and simple compounds.
Write formulae and balanced equations using conservation of mass, including half equations.
Write formulae and equations from a supplied Periodic Table.
Use common ion formulae to deduce compound formulae.
Construct balanced ionic equations.
Describe states with state symbols.
Describe tests for oxygen, hydrogen, carbon dioxide and chlorine.
Recall and use the Avogadro constant and the mole.
Explain how mass relates to moles, in both directions.
Explain how solute mass and solution volume give concentration.
Recall and use the law of conservation of mass.
Explain mass changes in open systems using the particle model.
Deduce an equation's stoichiometry from masses and explain limiting reactants.
Use a balanced equation to calculate masses of reactants or products.
Tell endothermic from exothermic reactions by surroundings' temperature change.
Draw and label reaction profiles for both types.
Explain activation energy as energy needed for a reaction.
Calculate energy change from bond-making and bond-breaking energies.
Explain oxidation and reduction as gain or loss of oxygen.
Explain oxidation and reduction as loss or gain of electrons.
Recall that acids give hydrogen ions and alkalis hydroxide ions in water.
Describe neutralisation as acid plus alkali or base giving salt and water.
Recognise neutralisation as hydrogen ions reacting with hydroxide ions to make water.
Recall acid reactions with carbonates and metals and write balanced equations.
Use and explain dilute, concentrated, weak and strong for acids.
Recall that pH measures relative acidity and alkalinity.
Describe neutrality, acidity and alkalinity by hydrogen ion concentration and pH.
Use the idea that tenfold more hydrogen ions lowers pH by one.
Describe techniques and apparatus for measuring pH.
Recall which products form at cathode and anode with inert electrodes.
Predict products of electrolysis of molten binary ionic compounds.
Describe competing reactions in electrolysis of aqueous solutions.
Describe electrolysis through ions present and electrode reactions.
Describe electrolysis with inert and non-inert electrodes.

units.title: Topic C4: Predicting and identifying chemical products

outcomes.text: Recall simple properties of Groups 1, 7 and 0.
Explain how group properties depend on outer electrons and predict trends.
Predict reactions and reactivity from Periodic Table position.
Explain how metal reactivity with water or acid relates to forming positive ions.
Deduce a reactivity order of metals from experiments.

units.title: Topic C5: Monitoring and controlling chemical reactions

outcomes.text: Suggest practical methods for finding reaction rate.
Interpret rate graphs and gradients.
Describe effects of temperature, concentration, pressure and surface area on rate.
Explain effects of temperature, concentration and pressure with collision frequency and energy.
Explain effect of solid piece size using surface area to volume ratio.
Describe characteristics of catalysts and their effect on rate.
Identify catalysts in reactions.
Explain catalytic action through activation energy.
Recall that enzymes are biological catalysts.
Recall that some reactions can be reversed by changing conditions.
Recall that dynamic equilibrium means equal forward and reverse rates in a closed system.
Predict effects of changing conditions on equilibrium and suggest conditions to maximise product.
Explain industrial metal extraction using carbon's place in the reactivity series.
Explain why and how electrolysis extracts some metals.
Evaluate biological methods of metal extraction.
Describe the principles of a life-cycle assessment.
Interpret life-cycle assessment data.
Describe recycling a material for another use and why it is viable.
Evaluate factors affecting recycling decisions.
Describe separating crude oil by fractional distillation.
Explain this separation using molecular size and intermolecular forces.
Describe fractions as mixtures of CnH2n+2 compounds.
Recall that crude oil supplies hydrocarbons and petrochemical feedstock.
Explain modern life's reliance on hydrocarbons and that crude oil is finite.
Describe cracking to make more useful materials.

topics.title: C6.2 Interpreting and interacting with earth systems

outcomes.text: Interpret evidence for how the atmosphere first formed.
Describe how an oxygen-rich atmosphere developed.
Describe the greenhouse effect as radiation interacting with atmospheric matter.
Evaluate evidence for human causes of climate change and its uncertainties.
Describe effects of rising carbon dioxide and methane and how to mitigate them.
Describe sources of carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and particulates and their problems.
Describe methods for increasing potable water using separation techniques.
Describe how and why the atomic model has changed.
Describe the atom as a small positive nucleus surrounded by electrons.
Recall the typical size of atoms and small molecules.
Define density.
Explain density differences between states of matter using particle arrangement.
Apply density, mass and volume relationships to changes where mass is conserved.
Describe how mass is conserved in melting, freezing, evaporating, condensing and subliming.
Describe how physical changes differ from chemical ones because the material recovers its properties.

subtopics.title: Specific heat capacity and latent heat

outcomes.text: Describe how heating changes stored energy and raises temperature or changes state.
Define specific heat capacity and distinguish it from specific latent heat.
Apply the relationship between internal energy change, mass, specific heat capacity and temperature change.
Use specific latent heat and mass to calculate energy change.
Explain how gas molecule motion relates to temperature and pressure.
Explain how gas temperature and pressure relate at constant volume.
Describe how to measure distance and time in different situations.
Measure distance and time to calculate speed, including from graphs.
Use ratios and proportional reasoning to convert units and find rates.
Explain the vector-scalar distinction for displacement and distance, velocity and speed.
Relate differences in motion to distance-time and velocity-time graphs.
Interpret enclosed areas in velocity-time graphs.
Calculate average speed for non-uniform motion.
Apply formulae for distance, time and speed, in uniform motion and uniform acceleration.
Recall examples of interacting objects, such as electrostatics, gravity and magnetism.
Describe how interactions between pairs of objects produce a force on each.
Represent forces as vectors with free body diagrams.
Use vector diagrams to show resolution, resultant force and equilibrium.
Describe forces on an isolated object, including terminal velocity.
Describe how two or more forces lead to a resultant force.
Describe balanced forces with zero resultant, qualitatively.
Apply Newton's first law to explain motion at uniform velocity and changing speed.
Apply Newton's second law relating force, mass and acceleration.
Explain inertia as how hard it is to change velocity, and inertial mass.
Define momentum and describe momentum in collisions.
Use work = force times distance along the force and describe the energy transfer.
Calculate stored energy and transfers, converting newton-metres to joules.
Explain power as the rate of energy transfer.
Recall and apply Newton's third law in equilibrium and non-equilibrium situations.
Explain why uniform circular motion has a changing velocity, qualitatively.
Explain that stretching, bending or compressing needs more than one force.
Describe elastic and plastic deformation from stretching forces.
Describe the relationship between force and extension for a spring.
Describe linear and non-linear force-extension relationships.
Calculate a spring constant in linear cases.
Calculate work done in stretching.
Describe that all matter has a gravitational field, stronger for massive objects.
Define weight, how it is measured, and its link to gravitational field strength g.
Recall the acceleration in free fall.
Describe charge as a property of matter, positive and negative.
Describe producing static electricity and sparks by rubbing, and forces between charged objects.
Explain static phenomena through transfer of electrons.
Recall that current is the rate of flow of charge and what charge flow needs.
Recall that current is the same everywhere in a single closed loop.
Recall and use the relationship between charge, current and time.
Describe differences between series and parallel circuits.
Represent d.c. circuits using terminal conventions and standard symbols.
Recall that current depends on resistance and potential difference, with units.
Recall and apply the relationship between I, R and V.
Explain that resistance is constant in some resistors and changes with conditions in others.
Explain circuit designs that explore these effects.
Use graphs to tell whether circuit elements are linear or non-linear.
Relate curves to the function of circuit elements.
Explain why series resistors increase net resistance but parallel ones decrease it.
Calculate currents, potential differences and resistances in series and parallel circuits.
Explain d.c. circuits designed for measurement and testing.
Explain how power in a device relates to potential difference and current.
Apply equations for potential difference, current, charge, resistance, power and energy.
Describe attraction and repulsion between poles of permanent magnets.
Describe permanent and induced magnets.
Describe a magnet's field, including how strength and direction change.
Explain how a dipping compass relates to evidence of the Earth's core being magnetic.
Describe how a current creates a magnetic effect and the field directions.
Recall that field strength depends on current and distance from the conductor.
Explain how solenoids strengthen the magnetic effect.
Describe how a magnet and current-carrying conductor exert forces on each other.
Show Fleming's left-hand rule gives force, current and field orientations.
Apply the equation linking force on a conductor to flux density, current and length.
Explain how this force makes a motor rotate.
Describe waves by amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period.
Define wavelength and frequency.
Describe and apply the relationship between wavelength, frequency and wave velocity.
Apply formulae relating velocity, frequency and wavelength.
Describe differences between transverse and longitudinal waves.
Describe water ripples as transverse waves and sound in air as longitudinal.
Describe evidence that the wave travels, not the water or air.
Recall that electromagnetic waves are transverse and travel through space at the same speed.
Explain that electromagnetic waves transfer energy from source to absorber.
Apply frequency-wavelength relationships across the spectrum.
Describe the main groupings of the spectrum from long to short wavelength.
Describe that our eyes detect only a limited range.
Recall that light is an electromagnetic wave.
Give practical uses of radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma waves.
Describe hazards of ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays to body tissue.
Recall that radio waves are produced by or induce oscillations in circuits.
Recall that substances absorb, transmit, refract or reflect waves depending on wavelength.
Explain effects linked to different wave speeds in different substances.
Recall that nuclei hold protons and neutrons and each element has a characteristic positive charge.
Recall that isotopes differ in the number of neutrons.
Use nuclear notation to describe differences between isotopes.
Recall that unstable nuclei emit alpha, beta, neutrons and gamma radiation.
Relate each emission to changes in nuclear mass or charge.
Write balanced decay equations with nuclear symbols.
Balance equations for alpha, beta and gamma emission using masses and charges.
Recall that electron arrangements can change by absorbing or emitting radiation.
Recall that atomic and nuclear changes generate and absorb radiation over a wide frequency range.
Explain half-life and its link to random decay.
Calculate the net decline as a ratio after a whole number of half-lives.
Recall the penetration differences of alpha, beta and gamma radiation.
Recall the difference between contamination and irradiation and compare their hazards.
Describe that energy transfers in a system cause no net change to total energy.
Describe how energy is stored when a system changes in common situations.
Describe energy changes when a system is heated.
Calculate energy changes in a system, choosing the right equation.
Calculate energy for a moving body, a stretched spring and a raised object.
Describe, with examples, how energy dissipates into less useful stores.
Describe energy transfer from batteries or mains in domestic devices.
Describe how appliance power ratings relate to energy transferred.
Calculate energy efficiency of any transfer.
Describe ways to increase efficiency.
Explain ways of reducing unwanted energy transfer.
Describe how wall thickness and conductivity affect rate of cooling, qualitatively.
Recall typical speeds of wind, sound, walking, running and cycling.
Estimate sizes of everyday accelerations.
Use ratios and proportional reasoning to convert units and compute rates.
Explain methods of measuring human reaction times and typical results.
Explain factors affecting the distance a vehicle needs to stop in an emergency.
Explain the dangers of large decelerations.
Describe main energy sources on Earth, compare uses, and tell renewable from non-renewable.
Explain patterns and trends in the changing use of energy resources.
Recall that grid power moves at high voltage and is stepped down for local use.
Recall that step-up and step-down transformers change potential difference along the grid.
Explain why the national grid is an efficient way to transfer energy.
Recall that UK domestic supply is a.c. at 50 Hz and about 230 V.
Explain the difference between direct and alternating voltage.
Recall the functions of live, neutral and earth wires and the potential differences between them.
Explain why a live wire is dangerous even with the switch open, and the danger of live-to-earth connection.
